title: The ten days
hook: no days are dearer to Allah for good deeds than the first ten of Dhul Hijjah (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shawwal, and six more fasts after the month ends. Your line was six more.

Ramadan is usually the month that comes to mind first when the holiest days of the Islamic year come up, and its nights carry Laylat al-Qadr. But a hadith in Bukhari points somewhere else. It names a different stretch of days, about two months after Ramadan ends, at the start of the last month of the year, the month of pilgrimage. While pilgrims are heading for Mecca, everyone else, at home, is also in a season. Today: the ten days.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn 'Abbas reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said there are no days in which good deeds are more beloved to God than these, meaning the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah. The companions were startled. Not even striving in the path of God? Not even that, he said, except a man who goes out with his life and his wealth and comes back with nothing. An ordinary good deed, done in these ten days, is set beside the hardest sacrifice there is. Commentators also connect the days to the Qur'an. Surah Al-Fajr opens with an oath, by the dawn, and ten nights, and commentators going back to Ibn 'Abbas understood those ten nights as these. And Surah Al-Hajj speaks of remembering God's name on appointed days, which Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have explained as the ten. What do people do? More of what they already do: extra prayer, charity, reading, kindness. Some fast the first nine days. Others fast at least the ninth, the day of 'Arafah, when the pilgrims stand on the plain; a hadith in Sahih Muslim hopes that fast wipes away the faults of the year before and the year after. Some companions, Bukhari notes, used to walk through the markets in these days saying the takbir aloud, and people around them took it up. And a hadith in Muslim says that someone planning to offer a sacrifice for Eid shouldn't cut their hair or nails from the start of the month, a small mark in the body that the season has begun. The point isn't a new set of rules. It's a window: the same deeds, in a season when they weigh more.

segments.voice: Think of ten days, starting today, and choose one small good you could add to each: a text to someone who's lonely, a coin in a box, ten minutes of reading, picking up litter on the walk home. Picture doing it near the end, when you're tired; if it still fits, keep it. If you pray, you can make your intention now.
Dhul Hijjah. The month of pilgrimage, whose first ten days the hadith calls dearer to God for good deeds than any other days. Today's word.

original.note: Arabic: Dhul Hijjah, the month of the pilgrimage, the last month of the Hijri year.

trapdoor: what you thought: the days before Eid, a countdown.
what it means: a season when ordinary good deeds weigh more, for pilgrims and for everyone at home.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 969 from Ibn 'Abbas; Al-Fajr 89:2's ten nights read as these by commentators from Ibn 'Abbas on; and the fast of 'Arafah in Muslim 1162.
recall: the pilgrims' call: here I am, O God

chat.says: If you're not going on Hajj, does the pilgrimage month mean anything for you?
options: Yes, a hadith calls its first ten days the dearest to God for good deeds.
No, the ten days only count for pilgrims standing at 'Arafah.
Yes, everyone at home must fast all ten days, including Eid.
chat.meaning: In Bukhari, no days are dearer to God for good deeds than these ten; people at home keep them with prayer, charity and fasting.

Dhul Hijjah.meaning: the month of pilgrimage, the last of the year

'Arafah.meaning: the plain where pilgrims stand on the ninth

Al-Fajr.meaning: Surah eighty-nine, which opens: by the dawn, and ten nights

Ibn 'Abbas.meaning: a companion who reported and explained these days

notes: All hadith paraphrased; numbers from memory (Bukhari 969; Muslim 1162, 1977); confirm.
The reading of 89:2's ten nights as the first ten of Dhul Hijjah is the majority view among classical commentators, but others exist; stated as 'a long line of commentators'. Confirm.
Ibn 'Abbas on 22:28 'appointed days' as the ten: reported as a ta'liq in Bukhari; confirm.
The hair-and-nails ruling: schools differ on whether it is obligatory or recommended; script keeps it descriptive.
The hook says Ramadan's nights carry Laylat al-Qadr and that this hadith names different days; scholars discuss how the two compare (days vs nights). Confirm the framing is fair.
